video_title: Situational Awareness, Hyperscaler Earnings and Warsh: A Bottom for AI Stocks?
gist: Jordi Visser argues the forced unwind of the ~$45bn AI-focused hedge fund Situational Awareness (Leopold), whose book Citadel bought and Millennium bid on, was a high-probability cleansing event after the worst month ever for crowded hedge fund longs (GS VIP index -12% vs S&P) and tech momentum (-40% YTD). He pairs that with hyperscaler earnings that showed no capex cuts and ~$1.7trn of combined backlog to argue the AI trade is a better risk/reward here, while insisting the deeper change is permanent: AI has destroyed terminal-value visibility, pushed factor volatility structurally higher, and made past-correlation risk optimizers unreliable, so leverage and factor risk will decompress for a long time.

themes.theme: Situational Awareness unwind as a cleansing event

insights.claim: The hedge fund Situational Awareness, reported to have held about $45 billion of positions, was forced to seek capital and wind down after AI-trade losses, with Citadel buying its stock portfolio and Millennium Management also bidding — a sequence Visser says historically marks market bottoms.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A named, completed forced-seller event in the most crowded AI longs removes the largest marginal supply, which is the classic precondition for a tradeable low in that basket.
insights.quote: I just want to bring this up that this is the kind of thing that does mark bottoms normally.

insights.claim: Once prime brokers begin 'marketing' a distressed fund's long/short portfolio to buyers, the fund's positions become visible to the largest players who then hedge or front-run them — the mechanism Visser uses to explain why 7 of the month's 12% crowded-long drawdown happened in four days.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Explains why forced-liquidation drawdowns are front-loaded and violent, and why the tape typically stabilizes fast once the book has changed hands.
insights.quote: Basically, you're showing people po people other people's poker hands and they're going going to go out there and they're going to hedge their book or front it or do whatever.

insights.claim: Situational Awareness was reportedly up around 80% year to date, but half to three quarters of that gain sat in an illiquid private Anthropic position, so the fund could not convert paper gains into cash to meet collateral calls and had to sell its liquid book.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A template risk for any fund marking large private AI stakes: strong headline performance plus illiquid marks equals forced liquidation of the liquid sleeve when margin is called.

insights.claim: Bloom Energy relative to Adobe is Visser's proxy for Situational Awareness's book (rumored longs versus shorts, cross-checked against the last 13F), and that ratio has given back everything it gained — his evidence the unwind has largely run its course.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Gives a live, tradeable spread to monitor whether AI-long/software-short crowding is still being liquidated or has cleared.

insights.claim: Visser, who traded through LTCM, the 2007 GARP quant unwind and Archegos, says this episode is a mix of all three but closest to Archegos — an event after which the market went higher — and explicitly excludes Melvin Capital as a comparison.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Sets the analog: a positioning shock resolved by a dealer/multistrat balance sheet rather than a systemic credit unwind, which historically resolved upward.

insights.claim: Unlike LTCM, where global markets were already falling before the unwind, almost all markets outside the US are currently above and rising above their 200-day moving average — evidence this is a factor/positioning event rather than a global leverage event.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The absence of global confirmation argues against buying index-level crash protection for a positioning-driven drawdown.

insights.claim: The Wednesday of the unwind printed the largest 2pm-to-4pm E-mini S&P futures volume of the entire year outside June 4th, consistent with roughly $15-20 billion of positions being sold and hedged into the close, and the S&P's 120-point drop that day was fully recovered the next session.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Identifies the liquidation as a mechanical, one-day futures hedge rather than a fundamental repricing, which is why the index snapped back immediately.

insights.claim: The collision of Fed week, major hyperscaler earnings with a live capex-cut rumor, and the end of a brutal momentum month is what pushed Situational Awareness over the edge, because managers were forced to defend a week of binary catalysts on a short chip stack.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Event-clustered weeks after a drawdown are when levered positioning breaks — a calendar risk to monitor rather than a fundamental one.

insights.claim: Hedge fund strategies were still up more than 10% on average for the year going into the unwind, and Visser's 'chip stack' framework says funds sitting on gains hedge and survive rather than fully liquidate — a reason to expect decompression rather than a cascade.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Year-to-date P&L is the best single predictor of whether stressed positioning gets hedged or dumped; positive chip stacks cap downside contagion.
insights.quote: hedge fund strategies were still on average up more than 10% for the year

insights.claim: The Goldman Sachs VIP hedge fund crowded-position index fell 12% relative to the S&P 500 for the month through Wednesday — the worst relative month since the index began in 2001, worse than the month of Lehman and roughly double any other month.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A historic outlier in crowded-long performance, achieved with the index flat, quantifies how much of the damage was positioning rather than fundamentals.

insights.claim: Seven of the 12% relative drawdown in crowded hedge fund longs occurred in the four sessions from Friday to Wednesday, the worst four-day rate of change on record including COVID — and it happened while the S&P was roughly flat and the VIX was low.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that index-level volatility gauges now completely miss factor-level stress, so hedges must be built at the factor, not index, level.

insights.claim: The technology momentum factor was down 40% year to date as of Thursday morning, worse than anything during the dotcom bust by almost 20% except for a single month in that era.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Puts the drawdown beyond dotcom extremes, supporting a mean-reversion or at least stabilization trade in the factor rather than fresh shorts.

insights.claim: Hedge funds sold more technology in this episode than at any point in Goldman's ten-year record, momentum factor volatility hit its highest in 45 years outside a recession, and gross and net exposure fell from five- and four-year highs to the middle of the pack over six weeks.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Exposure is now mid-range rather than extreme, reducing the fuel for further mechanical selling in tech.

insights.claim: Hedge fund leverage was at all-time highs per SEC Form PF data through Q3 2025 and Goldman recorded the largest cumulative gross leverage build since it began tracking in 2016 during the first five months of this year, with the buildup spanning equities and not just the fixed income basis trade.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Equity-side leverage at records is the transmission channel from factor volatility to liquidity risk, and it is what prime brokers will now ration.

themes.theme: Structurally higher factor vol as permanent regime change

insights.claim: The Morgan Stanley tech momentum factor's 30- and 60-day realized volatility is around 110 versus prior highs near 70, which annualizes to roughly 6-7% daily moves in a dollar-long/dollar-short book — a level Visser says makes re-risking to old exposures impossible.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Vol-targeted books must run structurally smaller factor bets, so the natural bid for crowded AI longs is permanently reduced even if prices recover.

insights.claim: An equal-weighted composite of the 60-day volatility of market-neutralized beta, quality, momentum and value factors sits at 38, above anything in its history, and the same measure relative to the sixth VIX futures contract is at 36 and still trending higher.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Any risk-weighted or optimized portfolio must cut factor exposure mechanically, and six-month S&P volatility looks cheap against realized factor volatility.

insights.claim: Factor volatility ran between 5 and 15 from 2000 to 2020 and has run 15 to 30 since, which Visser reads as a regime shift rather than an overshoot — he no longer believes it mean reverts.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If factor vol is permanently double its old range, quant capacity, leverage and crowded-trade sizing all reset lower for years.
insights.quote: The one thing that I do think is an absolute guarantee is that the market structure has changed forever

insights.claim: Equity-level implied volatility (VXEQ) has broken away from index implied volatility (VIX) starting right around the launch of ChatGPT, and Visser expects single-stock vol to stay rich to index vol because companies can now go out of business very quickly.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Express AI-disruption risk in single-name or dispersion trades, not S&P or NASDAQ puts, which is where Visser says smart people have been wasting money.

insights.claim: Visser's base case is no major credit event but a long, drawn-out deleveraging with multiple compression and disappointment, because prime brokers will not re-extend leverage while factor volatility stays elevated.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Argues for owning fundamentals and avoiding crowded levered factor exposure rather than positioning for a systemic blowup.
insights.quote: I don't think the prime brokers are going to allow leverage to go to the levels they have because I don't think the volatility that we saw is coming down.

insights.claim: From conversations with the Fed's risk group, Visser says the only two groups with enough leverage to turn this into a credit event are insurance companies and hedge funds.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Narrows systemic-risk monitoring to insurer asset marks and hedge fund leverage rather than banks, and insurers are where he suspects mispriced assets.
insights.quote: the only two areas when I've spoken to the risk group at the Fed that I'm worried about, I'm worried about insurance companies and I'm worried about hedge funds

insights.claim: Visser's causal chain for the new regime: AI compresses economic time so that a decade of innovation happens in a year, terminal value becomes unestimable for code-based businesses like Adobe and Salesforce, multiples compress, and stocks can fall 40% with no change in earnings.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Explains why valuation-based longs in software keep failing and why earnings-based screens miss the real risk being repriced.
insights.quote: Tokenization is here. Terminal value is gone forever.

insights.claim: Ubiquitous AI risk tools create a false sense of safety because optimizers are built on past correlations and past volatility, which Visser says are no longer relevant — he calls it a bubble in optimization.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Portfolios that look hedged on backward-looking optimizers are the ones most exposed to the next speed crash — a source of repeatable forced-selling.
insights.quote: This is like watching people drive down the street with all-wheel drive when it's icy and snowy out, thinking that they're protected.

insights.claim: Visser's May paper 'Bubbles, parabolas and speed crashes' predicted exactly this pattern: because AI compresses time, markets will produce more bubbles, more parabolic moves and more speed crashes, and the retail energy that chased the last move will not return soon.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Position sizing and stop discipline matter more than direction; expect repeated violent air pockets rather than a single cyclical bear.
insights.quote: There's going to be more speed crashes, guys, than there ever have been.

insights.claim: Robinhood has released an AI trading agent that reads charts, RSI, MACD and 16 more indicators, giving retail the same tooling as quant hedge funds, which Visser cites as proof AI agents are already here and as fuel for more speed crashes.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Democratized quant tooling means signal crowding now includes retail, compressing the time between signal and exhaustion.

themes.theme: Hyperscaler earnings kill the capex-cut thesis

insights.claim: Visser's single highest-conviction call, which he ranks as the most important of everything he publishes, is that compute demand is insatiable and that there is no way for supply to keep up, with no indications otherwise — everything bearish he hears rests instead on fear of overbuilding without revenues.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: This is the anchor of his whole book: as long as the supply/demand imbalance holds, drawdowns in AI infrastructure names are positioning events to buy rather than thesis breaks.
insights.quote: Compute demand is insatiable. There is no way for the supply side to keep up with the demand of Q compute currently and there are no indications that that's case.

insights.claim: No hyperscaler cut capex this quarter despite widespread expectations: Microsoft said customer demand continues to exceed available capacity and that in-quarter Azure capacity was quickly monetized, Sundar Pichai said Google remains supply constrained, and Zuckerberg said Meta is not building compute ahead of uncertain demand because demand already exists.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The single biggest bear catalyst for AI capex names failed to materialize, removing the main fundamental argument for staying short semis and power names.
insights.quote: customer demand continues to exceed available capacity

insights.claim: Amazon told investors that even at its planned capex it will not have enough capacity to meet all demand in 2026 and expects the same in 2027, that the lion's share of AWS 2027 compute capacity is already reserved, and that demand already booked for 2028 is striking.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Multi-year reserved capacity converts capex from a speculative bet into contracted revenue visibility, which is the direct rebuttal to the overbuild thesis.
insights.quote: The lion share of AWS 2027 compute capacity is already reserved.

insights.claim: Reported backlogs are $500 billion at Amazon, $500 billion at Google and $700 billion at Microsoft — about $1.7 trillion combined — with Google's backlog at 496 growing triple digits year over year.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A $1.7trn contracted backlog is the hard number to weigh against overbuild fears and to size the downstream revenue pool for semis, memory, power and optics.

insights.claim: Google disclosed that all sequential commercial RPO growth was driven by commitments from customers outside frontier model companies and that the majority of backlog is typical GCP contracts for a broad customer mix — directly undercutting the circular-revenue bear case.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If demand growth comes from enterprises rather than the labs, the vendor-financing/circularity critique loses its strongest empirical support.

insights.claim: Meta could have pleased investors by renting out its compute and appeared to leak that it would, then declined — which Visser reads as evidence Meta believes personal agents will consume that compute internally sooner than the market expects.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A revealed-preference signal that internal agent demand is real; also removes an expected new source of merchant compute supply.

insights.claim: With 60% of the S&P 500 reported, sales growth is running 14% with broad earnings growth across every sector and estimate revisions still rising — the longest such stretch in five years — which Visser says makes being bearish stocks unprofitable.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Positive revision breadth alongside a factor unwind argues the drawdown was positioning, and supports buying fundamentally sound names that got hit.
insights.quote: It's like it doesn't pay to be to be bearish stocks when this is going on.

insights.claim: Weekly DRAM spot prices for older, non-leading-edge memory going back to 2016 are still rising every week with the historical cyclicality absent, which Visser presents as physical confirmation that data-center buildout is not slowing.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A high-frequency, hard-to-fake indicator of AI buildout that can be tracked weekly to confirm or falsify the capex-slowdown narrative.

themes.theme: AI lab revenue ramp versus circularity risk

insights.claim: On the All-In podcast David Sacks said Anthropic's annualized revenue is $74 billion at the halfway point of the year and implied it grows roughly 10x again to over $100 billion, with OpenAI on pace for about $75 billion — approximately $175 billion from two companies that had zero revenue two years ago.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser (relaying David Sacks on the All-In Podcast)
insights.so_what: Frames the ROIC debate: lab revenue of this scale alongside roughly $2 trillion of cloud revenue makes the 'no revenues' critique quantitatively hard to sustain.
insights.quote: Guys, that's 175 billion in revenues from two companies that had zero two years ago.

insights.claim: Sacks argued there is an unlimited appetite for on-demand intelligence with no upper bound as long as models keep improving, a view Visser says he completely agrees with.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser (relaying David Sacks)
insights.so_what: If demand is genuinely unbounded relative to supply, compute pricing power sits with whoever owns installed capacity.
insights.quote: As far as I'm concerned there is an unlimited appetite for ondemand intelligence. I don't think there's an upper bound for how much intelligence you can tap as long as it continues to get better.

insights.claim: On Invest Like the Best, Sam Altman said OpenAI's conviction to secure massive compute came from observing an exponential model improvement curve around GPT-4, that supply is the bottleneck today, and that the biggest near-term compute gains may come from software efficiency rather than hardware.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser (relaying Sam Altman on Invest Like the Best)
insights.so_what: Software-efficiency gains are the nearest-term risk to the compute-scarcity trade, so watch inference cost curves as the leading indicator.

insights.claim: Visser argues the only two paths for compute supply to catch demand — agents squeezing more intelligence out of existing compute, and physical-world robotics expanding the whole supply chain — cannot happen within the next year, so scarcity persists.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Defines a roughly one-to-two-year window in which owners of installed compute retain pricing power, and identifies the two signals that would end it.

insights.claim: Visser says the real bear risk was highest in October of last year, when the danger was that labs spent heavily and enterprises never adopted; that risk was invalidated because AI agents arrived at least a year earlier than expected, making inference demand insatiable.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reframes the bear case as already having failed on adoption timing — the reason Visser built his agentic thematic portfolio before the move.

insights.claim: Visser dismisses the open-source disruption argument on hardware grounds: Chinese model companies are tiny and their models still must run on someone's compute, so open-source demand routes back through the hyperscalers via platforms like Bedrock.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Open-weight model progress is bullish, not bearish, for cloud and compute owners because inference has to be hosted somewhere.

insights.claim: Visser concedes the genuine risk that AI spending is circular and that Anthropic, OpenAI or Meta could fail if revenue does not arrive, singling out Meta as making a huge bet with nothing to show yet, and says widening credit spreads for these borrowers are rational.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Defines the actual bear tail as a funding/credit event at a specific borrower rather than a demand shortfall, which is where hedges belong.

themes.theme: Token efficiency as the new moat

insights.claim: Visser highlights a widely read contrarian piece arguing that expensive compute converts token efficiency into pricing power and widens the frontier premium, so the moat becomes access to compute plus the ability to charge for efficiency.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reverses the commoditization thesis: scarce compute makes the best model more valuable, not less, which changes how to value frontier labs versus cheap challengers.
insights.quote: His argument is that expensive compute converts token efficiency into pricing power, widens the frontier premium.

insights.claim: Visser's gas-and-cars analogy for why the best model wins when compute is expensive: at $1 a gallon nobody cares about mileage, at $10 everyone pays a premium for efficiency — so a cheaper model like Kimi K3.0 loses to a more token-efficient frontier model.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A usable heuristic for model-layer competition: price per token matters far less than tokens per task when compute is the binding constraint.
insights.quote: If gas is a dollar a gallon, nobody cares about the fuel efficiency. When it's $10, everyone pays a premium for the car with the best mileage.

insights.claim: Visser says token efficiency, not token maxing, is now the story, and cites it as the reason he has written so much about Vera Rubin, while noting SpaceX as another example of what owning your own compute enables.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Points hardware selection toward next-generation platforms optimized for efficiency per token as the investable expression of the thesis.
insights.quote: We're getting into a situation where token efficiency is the story, not token maxing.

insights.claim: Gavin Baker argues the market is overreacting to widening hyperscaler credit spreads and that the missing piece is GPU rental spot prices being at least twice contract rates, with $60 billion per gigawatt implying $1.5-2.2 trillion of capex against roughly $1.3 trillion of consensus hyperscaler cash flow.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser (relaying Gavin Baker)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the funding gap driving hyperscaler bond issuance while the spot-versus-contract GPU spread shows scarcity is real and monetizable.

insights.claim: Visser estimates it will be at least another two years before enough hardware exists for everyone to run open-source models locally, which he says is more than enough runway for hyperscaler AI revenue to arrive.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Gives an explicit time horizon for the compute-scarcity trade and the point at which the disruption risk to cloud economics becomes live.

themes.theme: Technical setup and how Visser is re-risking

insights.claim: Visser is using the follow-through day framework — a major index rising meaningfully on higher volume, typically on days four through ten of a rally attempt — to distinguish an investable rally from a short-covering pop, and notes the day after the low had the biggest volume since June and closed above the prior day's highs.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated confirmation test for the low: hold the lows and build time over the next six to seven sessions, or the unwind is not finished.
insights.quote: a follow-through day is confirmation that an oversold bounce may be turning into a real investable rally rather than just a short covering pop

insights.claim: SMH broke below the neckline of a head-and-shoulders formation, trapping new shorts, then gapped back above it — a failed breakdown Visser treats as the key technical event in semis, with the lows as the critical reference level.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Gives a defined invalidation level for long semis exposure: a loss of those lows breaks the cleansing-event thesis.

insights.claim: Visser's 63-day rate of change on his thematic portfolio went from more than +50% in May to -1.7% now, meaning the excess has been worked off in both price and time — the condition he requires before adding risk.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A reusable rule for the AI complex: reduce risk when three-month rate of change is historically extended, add when it has reverted in both price and time.
insights.quote: I do believe markets move on a rate of change basis and it pays to reduce risk when you get above historic levels.

insights.claim: Visser cut Micron progressively from mid-May, holds about one fifth of his May position size, is buying below $900 despite the stock trading near $850 against a 200-day around $500, and expects $1,500-1,600 within a year while admitting he is not convinced the absolute low is in.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A live, sized example of scaling into a drawdown rather than calling the bottom, with an explicit target and a much better risk/reward than in May.
insights.quote: my micron position right now is about 1/5if of the size that it was in May when I was getting out of it

insights.claim: Beneath the factor carnage, breadth stayed healthy: 67 new highs in the S&P yesterday (the most since February), 72% of the S&P above its 50-day, 68% above its 20-day, and the month finished unchanged with seven sectors up and four down.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Broad participation during a record factor unwind is the strongest argument that this was a positioning event and not the start of a bear market.
insights.quote: this is a bull market still. 67 new highs in the S&P yesterday, the most since February.

insights.claim: NDX relative to the S&P had its worst month since the dotcom bubble and NDX RSI hit its lowest level of the past year, mirroring the prior instance when the index gapped higher the following day.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Historic relative underperformance plus washed-out momentum oscillators is the setup for a tech-versus-index mean-reversion trade.

insights.claim: Visser's 'combing through the rubble' screen requires two conditions — price above the 200-day moving average and the 200-day itself still rising — then ranks names by how far below their 20- and 50-day they have fallen, which is how he found AOI, and he cross-checks earnings commentary before buying.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A repeatable post-crash screen that separates structurally intact names from broken ones, with the rising 200-day as the structural filter.
insights.quote: I want the uh price above the 200 day moving average. Think Micron, the 200 day moving average is somewhere 500. We're still around 850. And I want the 200 day itself still rising.

insights.claim: Roughly 74% of AI-related positions remain above their 200-day moving average and 84 of the 100 names in Visser's universe still have a rising 200-day slope, which he cites as evidence no structural damage was done to the AI trade.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Distinguishes a valuation/positioning drawdown from a trend break, supporting adds rather than exits in the AI complex.

insights.claim: Corning, one of Visser's ten concentrated names correlated to the 100-name index, round-tripped all the way back to the closing price of the day Meta announced a $6 billion deal with it — roughly 100 million homes' worth of optical fiber — and it also announced an Nvidia partnership.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete example of the screen's logic: a contracted, quantifiable AI order that the market has fully de-rated back to pre-announcement levels.

insights.claim: Visser's confirmation window is explicit: how the market trades over the next six to seven days matters most, and if the panic lows do not hold, something bigger is going on and hedge funds could still be massively unwinding.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Gives a dated, falsifiable test for the cleansing-event thesis, with the panic low as the stop for AI-trade adds.
insights.quote: how we trade over the next six to seven days, there should be back and forth, but use that followth through day approach

themes.theme: Warsh Fed, dollar positioning and credit cracks

insights.claim: The Fed under Kevin Worsh held rates at three, exactly what Wall Street expected despite some strategists floating 50 basis points, yet markets remain vexed — Visser argues the dovish/hawkish framing no longer applies because Worsh wants to replace revised, backward-looking academic data with forward-looking indicators.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Trading this Fed off traditional dove/hawk reaction functions will misfire; the reaction function itself is being rewritten.
insights.quote: The Fed is not the same Fed and this whole dovish hawkish thing is not there.

insights.claim: With the 10-year near 4.70, 10-year inflation swap rates down since Worsh arrived and August inflation expectations around zero, Visser reads the Fed's position as the market having tightened for it — real yields up, inflation down — allowing it to sit and wait.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If market-implied inflation keeps falling, the bar for hikes stays high regardless of hawkish rhetoric — a reason the surprise-hike scare was mispriced.

insights.claim: Crowded long dollar positioning is at its highest level in four years while the dollar has already softened on BOJ speculation, with Jackson Hole and possible dollar-yen intervention as catalysts — and Visser notes dollar turns have recently clustered at roughly three-month intervals (end of January, April, July).
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Extreme crowded dollar longs into a known catalyst is the setup for a dollar-down move, which he says is bullish gold and silver.

insights.claim: Visser is unconcerned by hyperscaler CDS but flags that the triple-C option-adjusted spread has a bad-looking roll to it and is diverging from high yield, because weak credit typically leads and eventually drags everything in.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Names the specific credit indicator to watch as the potential regime-changer, and rules out the Mag 7 CDS scare as a false signal.
insights.quote: the way credit usually goes is the weak start going up and it eventually drags everything in

insights.claim: Visser expects more private credit problems because of the scale of capital AI is absorbing and the disruption it is causing, notes the CCC divergence began around when software stocks broke, and flags the Dodgers-Guggenheim-Mark Walter private credit story plus mispriced insurance-industry assets as things to read and watch.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Points the credit-stress search at private credit and insurers rather than banks, aligning with his view on who holds dangerous leverage.

insights.claim: Visser says he was told repeatedly he was wrong on Google and that the stock would collapse after closing below its 200-day, but argues the market is ignoring a backlog that makes the company's numbers insane and expects Google to take off from here.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A specific named long where he says sentiment and the reported backlog diverge, and the stock has already recovered off the earnings dip.
insights.quote: I am shocked how many people don't care about the backlog of Google and tell me it doesn't mean anything.

insights.claim: Visser pushes back on the view that China plans to make AI free for the rest of the world, pointing to the Ezra Klein interview with former Australian prime minister Kevin Rudd on Xi Jinping, and says applying a Marxist-Leninist plus Schumpeterian lens to that balance of power is why he cares so much about Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A geopolitical input for the open-source-versus-frontier debate and for the case that state-directed AI competition supports non-sovereign stores of value.
